Empirical Research Plan – “Do departures from trade‐policy neutrality raise welfare in developing economies?”

================================================================
1. Identification Strategy
----------------------------------------------------------------
Primary approach:  Staggered Difference-in-Differences (DID) with an event-study decomposition a la Sun & Abraham (2021) / Callaway & Sant’Anna (2020), complemented by a shift-share instrumental-variables extension (Bartik-type IV).

Why appropriate

•  The research question is inherently comparative—what happens to the same country before vs. after it adopts a purposely **non-neutral** policy stance, relative to countries that do not change stance in the same years.  
•  1980-2004 panel coverage (≈ 25 years, > 100 countries) supplies the multiple pre- and post-periods needed to test pre-trends and dynamic effects.  
•  Policy “shocks” (large changes in tariff levels/dispersion, introduction or repeal of targeted subsidies, or FDI tax-holiday packages) occurred at different times across countries ⇒ staggered treatment.  
•  Shift-share IV—worldwide commodity-specific tariff cuts interacted with each country’s pre-existing import composition—provides quasi-exogenous variation in tariff levels/dispersion that helps address policy endogeneity and supplies over-identification for robustness.

================================================================
2. Treatment and Control
----------------------------------------------------------------
Treatment variable  
    • Binary indicator  POLICY_INTENSIVE_ct  that switches from 0 to 1 in the first year t that country c moves **away from neutrality**. Operationalised as:

        (a)  A fall in the *uniform-tariff index* (simple average tariff) < 15% *and*  
        (b)  An *increase* in the coefficient of variation (CoV) of industry tariffs by ≥ 0.15 *or* the enactment of at least one sector-specific subsidy/FDI-tax incentive recorded in IMF Fiscal ROSCs.

    A switch must persist ≥ 3 consecutive years to be coded as a genuine policy regime change.

Control group  
    • Countries that never cross the threshold during 1980-2004 or do so only after the sample window (“never-treated” & “last-treated-late”).  
    • In robustness, we also use *not-yet-treated* countries in each event-time cell (per Sun–Abraham).

Treatment timing / event date  
    • EVENT_YEAR_c = first year that POLICY_INTENSIVE = 1 for country c. All subsequent years remain treated (absorbing treatment).

No running variable is needed (not an RDD).

================================================================
3. Key Identifying Assumptions
----------------------------------------------------------------
A1.  Parallel trends:  In the absence of non-neutral policy adoption, treated and control countries would have had parallel paths in productivity, GDP per capita, export sophistication, etc.  
        – Plausibility: Region×year and income-group×year fixed effects absorb global shocks; pre-trend graphs and placebo leads can be inspected. Mixed support expected—hence we augment with shift-share IV.  

A2.  No concurrent confounders:  Other reforms (e.g., democratization, macro-stabilization) that coincide exactly with policy-stance switches would bias estimates.  
        – Plausibility: Partly addressed via controls for IMF programs, WTO accession, PTAs, capital-account liberalisation indices.

A3.  Stable unit treatment value (SUTVA):  One country’s switch does not directly change another’s outcomes except through global prices already captured by year FE.  
        – Plausibility: Reasonable for most outcomes; we re-estimate excluding the largest economies (China, India).

A4.  Exogenous instrument validity (IV extension):  Import-share-weighted world tariff changes affect domestic outcomes only through induced domestic tariff/dispersion changes.  
        – Plausibility: World-level MFN tariff cuts are negotiated in multilateral rounds—unlikely to respond to an individual developing country’s growth prospects.

================================================================
4. Threats to Identification & Mitigation
----------------------------------------------------------------
T1. Policy endogeneity (reverse causality):  Governments may adopt selective interventions *because* growth is slowing.  
    • Mitigation:  (i) shift-share IV; (ii) include 3-year lags of growth as controls; (iii) drop obvious crisis episodes.  

T2. Violation of parallel trends:  If future-treated countries already diverge pre-event.  
    • Mitigation:  Event-study leads; propensity-score reweighting to create better-balanced synthetic control; difference-in-differences-matching.  

T3. Measurement error in tariff dispersion and subsidy data.  
    • Mitigation:  Use multiple sources (WITS, IMF, UNCTAD TRAINS, WTO notifications); instrument helps attenuate attenuation bias; perform IV-based reliability ratio correction.

================================================================
5. R Code Outline
----------------------------------------------------------------
```r
# ------------------------------------------------------------- #
# 0.  Libraries
library(data.table)
library(fixest)        # TWFE & event-study
library(did)           # Callaway–Sant’Anna estimator
library(ivreg)         # IV
library(ggplot2)

# ------------------------------------------------------------- #
# 1.  Load country-year data
dat <- fread("country_trade_policies_1980_2004.csv")

# ------------------------------------------------------------- #
# 2.  Variable construction
dat[, policy_dispersion := sd_industry_tariffs / mean_industry_tariffs]   # CoV
dat[, uniform_tariff := avg_statutory_tariff]

# Define treatment: switch when uniform tariff < 0.15 & dispersion ↑ ≥ .15
dat <- dat[order(country, year)]
dat[, treat_switch :=
       (uniform_tariff < 0.15 & policy_dispersion - shift(policy_dispersion, 3L, type = "lag") >= 0.15)]
dat[, POLICY_INTENSIVE := 0L]
dat[treat_switch == TRUE, EVENT_YEAR := year]
dat[, EVENT_YEAR := min(EVENT_YEAR, na.rm = TRUE), by = country]
dat[year >= EVENT_YEAR & !is.na(EVENT_YEAR), POLICY_INTENSIVE := 1L]

# Event-time dummies (-5 … +10)
for (k in -5:10)
    dat[, paste0("leads_lags_",k) := as.integer(year - EVENT_YEAR == k)]

# ------------------------------------------------------------- #
# 3.  Main TWFE regression with Sun & Abraham estimator
es_sa <- feols(log_TFP ~ sunab(EVENT_YEAR, year) + IMF_program + democracy_index
               | country + year, data = dat, cluster = ~country)
summary(es_sa)

# ------------------------------------------------------------- #
# 4.  Shift-share IV (Bartik) – first stage and 2SLS
# Instrument = sum_s (world_tariff_change_s,t * pre1980_import_share_c,s)
# Assume pre-computed as bartik_iv
dat <- merge(dat, fread("bartik_instrument.csv"), by = c("country","year"))
iv_mod <- ivreg(log_TFP ~ uniform_tariff + policy_dispersion + controls |
                          bartik_iv + controls, data = dat)
summary(iv_mod)

# ------------------------------------------------------------- #
# 5.  Robustness – exclude China & India
es_sa_noBig <- update(es_sa, subset = !(country %in% c("CHN","IND")))
etable(list(Base = es_sa, NoBig = es_sa_noBig))
```

================================================================
6. Expected Results
----------------------------------------------------------------
Theory offers ambiguous priors. Standard optimal-tax logic says *non-neutral* interventions generate static dead-weight losses; dynamic infant-industry or coordination stories can overturn this. My prior:

• Average developing-country effect of moving *away* from neutrality on log-TFP: β ≈ −0.02 to 0.00 (i.e., −2 % or statistically zero).  
• Heterogeneity: Positive (β ≈ +0.05) for high-state-capacity East Asian subgroup; negative (β ≈ −0.05) for low-capacity, commodity-exporting countries.

================================================================
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (Staggered DID/Event Study)
----------------------------------------------------------------
C1: Clear treatment definition, timing observable ………………… 1  
C2: Parallel pre-trends demonstrated graphically/statistically … 0.5 (needs testing)  
C3: No major simultaneous confounders ………………………………… 0.5  
C4: No anticipation or spillovers ………………………………………… 0.5  
C5: Robust standard errors & alternative estimators used …… 1  
TOTAL = 3.5 / 5  → Moderate internal validity

================================================================
The proposed design combines the strengths of staggered policy timing, modern DID estimators immune to heterogeneous treatment effects bias, and an orthogonal shift-share instrument to confront policy endogeneity, thereby yielding credible estimates of whether non-neutral trade‐cum-industrial policies promote or hinder welfare in developing economies.
